title: Mohnish Pabrai's Session with MIT's Brass Rat Investments on March 12, 2024
summary: Pabrai opens by asking why even Buffett and Munger found only about a dozen needle-moving investments in 58 years, and answers that the circle of competence expands slowly through ownership (See's taught them to buy Coke; railroads took years to understand), making investing a game of extreme patience plus extreme decisiveness. The Q&A, held days after Munger's memorial, covers Munger as a 'giver', Dakshana's swing-for-the-fences philanthropy, how he judged Sergio Marchionne and valued Fiat Chrysler (and missed holding Ferrari), why students have an edge spotting future 50-baggers, the Turkish Coke bottler as a macro-immune business, and his empty-calendar reading life.

ideas.idea: Even Buffett and Munger, working extremely hard, found only about a dozen needle-moving investments in 58 years, roughly one great idea every five years, which shows how rare true edge is.
ideas.detail: Buffett's 2023 letter said about 12 investments made Berkshire what it is; Pabrai guesses Coke, See's Candies, Burlington Northern, Cap Cities/ABC and the hiring of Ajit Jain. Munger was still placing buy orders six days before he died at 99.9.

ideas.idea: Your circle of competence starts narrow, limited to products you use, and expands only slowly by osmosis; be an inch wide and a mile deep rather than an inch deep and a mile wide.
ideas.detail: There is no prescribed way to enlarge the circle; it grows as you learn how the world works and through ownership experience.

ideas.idea: Owning See's Candies for years gave Buffett and Munger an education in brands and pricing power that they could not have gotten from analysis alone, and without it the Coke investment 13 years later would never have happened.
ideas.detail: They paid $25 million (three times book, and said they'd walk at $25,000,001) when the family wanted $30 million and admit they were barely smart enough to buy it. Buffett's only involvement was raising prices every January 1 by 10-15% against 3-5% inflation; volume still grew 1.5-2% a year. In 1988 Berkshire put a quarter of its book value into Coke.

ideas.idea: Coca-Cola is a far more complicated business than it appears and is still an emerging-market growth story 138 years after its 1886 founding, with the flagship brand still 70-80% of the pie.
ideas.detail: Unlike See's, which does not travel and has repeatedly failed to expand outside California, Coke travels well and has no aftertaste, so consumption propensity does not fall with use. The concentrate business Goizueta separated from bottling is like a software company: make it for a dollar, sell it for five or ten, and keep raising the price.

ideas.idea: Buffett and Munger were rightly negative on railroads for decades and were late to the party, but once they understood that double-stacking, labor efficiency and fuel prices had changed the economics, they had an edge no one else had and bought Burlington Northern.
ideas.detail: Railroads are regulated, capital-intensive common carriers forced to haul toxic chemicals at published prices. It took them several years to see the change; they bought the stock first and the whole company in late 2009.

ideas.idea: When Berkshire bought Coke in 1988 it was at a single-digit trailing multiple with two gifted managers shedding non-core junk and becoming a buyback machine, a lollapalooza where one plus one became eleven.
ideas.detail: Coke had bought movie studios and shrimp farms in Thailand. The same 'huge delta between past and future' insight applied to railroads, to utilities under Greg Abel and David Sokol, and to insurance under Ajit Jain. GEICO had 2% US auto share when Berkshire took control and is now double-digit, knocking on the door of the largest player.

ideas.idea: Investing is a game of extreme patience combined with extreme decisiveness: long periods where nothing is interesting, then a rare aha moment where you understand something better than the world and must go all in.
ideas.detail: Two or three big aha moments in an investing lifetime is doing well; they don't last long, and the combination of patience and decisiveness does not come naturally to most humans. Looking back over almost 30 years he can see the moments where it was obvious to step up and go big.

ideas.idea: Once you do the work, intrinsic value becomes obvious; many aha moments will turn out to be fake, but if you set criteria and keep digging you will occasionally see something the other seven billion people cannot.
ideas.detail: Warren and Charlie could see the gap between price and value at Coke quickly, but only because of prior experience with See's, buybacks and capital allocation. Seeing a multi-decade runway in 1988 has held up for 36 years.

ideas.idea: Be a giver, not a taker or a matcher, as Charlie Munger was: eliminate takers and matchers from your life and don't keep a scorecard, because the world figures out extractors.
ideas.detail: Cites Adam Grant's 'Give and Take'. Munger wanted 'I tried to be useful' on his gravestone; in 1965 he offered to help Buffett fix the Berkshire mistake with no ownership stake, which led to his becoming vice chairman 11-12 years later. He never missed a Costco board meeting in 27 years.

ideas.idea: Munger's other great lesson was total focus on the problem in front of him rather than looking back at his legacy, powered by relentless reading filed into a latticework of mental models.
ideas.detail: Into his late 90s he was searching for a Daily Journal CEO and designing UCSB dorms, asking how tall an F-150 is so it would fit the parking garage. He would answer Pabrai's Dakshana dilemmas before the question was finished, despite not knowing India, because he could pull from many models.

ideas.idea: Philanthropy has the opposite rules from investing: go high risk, high return, swing for the fences and don't care about a high probability of failure, as long as success moves the needle.
ideas.detail: The Gates Foundation has spent decades on vaccines with little to show, but a malaria vaccine would change the game as polio and smallpox did. He started Dakshana fully expecting the money to be torched for ten years before getting traction; instead it got traction in weeks and has never lost even $10,000.

ideas.idea: He cloned Buffett's giving formula: give a fixed percentage each year (2% of net worth from 2007, when it exceeded $50 million) so that compounding above the giving rate means the dollars given keep rising forever.
ideas.detail: Buffett gives 5% of his remaining Berkshire shares each year to four or five foundations; because intrinsic value grows faster than 5%, he'd still be giving more each year if he lived a thousand years. Pabrai's first-year giving in 2007 was about $1.3-1.4 million. He calls himself a shameless cloner.

ideas.idea: Keep separation of church and state: never mix investing with saving the planet, because the two mindsets are different and combining them won't get you to the promised land.
ideas.detail: When he looks at philanthropy he looks only at philanthropy, and when investing only at investing; Dakshana is focused solely on social impact, whose return on invested capital is so extreme that the next five ventures could fail and it would still be fine.

ideas.idea: Judging management is straightforward: ignore what they say will happen and look only at the track record of what has happened.
ideas.detail: Sergio Marchionne had eight years of history at Fiat, Harvard cases and a book on the Agnelli family; Fiat had cycled through five CEOs in 12 months and was losing over $1 million a day when he arrived. He copied Lee Iacocca's Chrysler playbook of replacing inherited direct reports with 30-somethings pulled from deep in the organization.

ideas.idea: Fiat Chrysler was a simple sum of bulletproof franchises: with a $5 billion market cap, Ram alone and Jeep alone would each produce more than $5 billion a year in cash flow, giving a valuation more than 10 times the stock price.
ideas.detail: Marchionne published five-year guidance for 2017-18 that implied a P/E below one, and nobody believed him even in black and white. Ram, Jeep and minivans were oligopoly franchises; the rest, including 80% of Ferrari, Maserati and Alfa Romeo, could be tossed in for free.

ideas.idea: Students have a big edge over him in finding future 50-baggers because they adopt change first, so make a list of every public company you pay even $1 a year to and work that list.
ideas.detail: College students cut landlines first, knew Facebook 8-10 years before old people, and went to Chipotle before the rest of the world. Cell phones were once thought to saturate at 2% of the population and are now near 100%. Fast forward 10-20 years and that list of companies you already pay will contain 50-baggers.

ideas.idea: He is the wrong person to ask about AI, but from the periphery its impact looks transformational everywhere and it has probably already obsoleted the stock photography business.
ideas.detail: Cites an app that converts an Indian-accented outsourced worker's voice into an American accent; says MIT students sitting at the front lines of the change have a far better view than he does from Austin.

ideas.idea: When something doesn't make sense to you, stop, take notes and go down the rabbit hole, because investing is the business of drilling down on anomalies, as Seinfeld does with a yellow pad for comedy.
ideas.detail: He hated the auto industry (unionized, high capex, consumer taste) but seeing Ted Weschler and David Einhorn in General Motors made no sense to him, so he investigated and it led to the Fiat Chrysler home run. Seinfeld's book 'Is This Anything?' describes noting every human anomaly; most don't pan out, some do.

ideas.idea: His big mistake in the Fiat Chrysler home run was selling Ferrari, which he dismissed as a $3-4 billion afterthought and which became almost a 25-bagger, roughly $400-500 million on a $20 million investment.
ideas.detail: Ferrari was earning a quarter billion a year and he was focused on the pieces that would earn the market cap in a single year; he made 5-6x on Ferrari but it should never have been sold. He missed it despite looking carefully for years.

ideas.idea: Starting top-down from politics, elections or macro is the wrong way; start with a business, and look for businesses immune to macro when a country is hated and cheap.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: He went to Turkey because it was dislocated and unloved, visited 70-80 listed Turkish businesses over a few years, ignored the macro and looked for the greatest businesses. The lira went from 5 to 32 per dollar in five years and his dollar investments are still up massively.

ideas.idea: A Coke bottler survives even a thermonuclear event that wipes out 99.99% of humanity, because someone will always trade some labor for an eight-ounce serving of Coke regardless of inflation, currency or exchange rates.
ideas.detail: This is why he owns the Turkish Coke bottler and doesn't care about the lira; the business is immune to the macro that everyone else is fixated on.

ideas.idea: Be extremely good at saying no, keep an empty calendar with no predetermined agenda, and let each day be spent either deep in a rabbit hole or reading in search of the next one.
ideas.detail: The only thing on his calendar that day was the MIT session, and nothing was scheduled the next day. Investment reading takes priority; he has read a quarter to a third of his library, is a harsh grader, and believes most 300-page books contain five pages of content, so he abandons books that don't grab him, unlike Bill Gates who finishes every book.

ideas.idea: Work backward from your eulogy: if something is not going to make it into the one-and-a-half page eulogy your best friend reads at your funeral, why are you spending time on it?
ideas.detail: Buffett and Munger are good at getting to the essence; lunches and coffees that people want just take away focus. Less is more.
